title: Streaming Billions of Hours
description: Design a video streaming system from upload to playback — transcoding pipelines, adaptive bitrate, CDN delivery, and live streaming challenges.

segments.text: Five hundred hours of video are uploaded to YouTube every minute. Netflix serves over one billion hours of video monthly. Let's design the system that makes this possible.

It starts with upload. A creator uploads a raw video file — potentially gigabytes. The upload service handles chunked uploads with resumability. If the connection drops at ninety percent, the creator doesn't start over.

Raw video can't be served directly. Transcoding converts the original into multiple formats and resolutions: 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K. Each resolution gets encoded in multiple codecs like H.264 and VP9. That's dozens of output files per video.

Transcoding is a directed acyclic graph of tasks. Split the video into segments, transcode each segment in parallel across many machines, then stitch the results. A two-hour movie can be transcoded in minutes instead of hours.
You're watching a video on the train. You enter a tunnel, bandwidth drops from ten megabits to one megabit per second. The video should keep playing smoothly.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you handle bandwidth fluctuations without buffering?

segments.text: Adaptive Bitrate Streaming. The video is split into small segments, typically two to ten seconds each. Each segment exists in multiple quality levels. The player monitors bandwidth and switches quality segment by segment. Seamless.

A manifest file, like an HLS playlist, lists all available segments and quality levels. The player downloads the manifest first, then fetches segments one by one, choosing the best quality its current bandwidth can support.

Serving video from one data center would be impossibly slow for global users. CDNs cache video segments at edge locations worldwide. A viewer in Tokyo gets segments from a Tokyo edge server, not from a US origin. Latency drops dramatically.

Not all videos are equal. Popular videos are cached aggressively on CDN edges. Long-tail content lives in origin storage and gets pulled to edge only on demand. Netflix pre-positions popular titles at edge locations before peak viewing hours.
Everything we've discussed works for pre-recorded video. But what about live streaming? A soccer match is happening right now, and millions of viewers want to watch with minimal delay.
segments.thought_prompt: How would live streaming change the architecture when you can't pre-transcode or pre-cache content?

segments.text: Live streaming flips the pipeline. Transcoding happens in real-time as the stream arrives. Segments are encoded and pushed to CDN edges within seconds. The trade-off is higher latency — typically five to thirty seconds — and less time for quality optimization.

Video streaming is a pipeline: upload, transcode in parallel, store in multiple qualities, serve via CDN with adaptive bitrate. Live streaming adds real-time transcoding. The CDN is the hero — without edge caching, streaming at global scale would be impossible.
